passages.title: Oppression and the midwives
passages.summary: A new king enslaves Israel. Shiphrah and Puah refuse his order to kill boys.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how reverence for God can require resistance to cruelty.

contextNote.title: Forced work and fear
contextNote.text: Pharaoh treats a growing people as a threat. He turns that fear into forced work and killing. The store cities serve royal interests. The women resist through small acts that preserve life. The book begins with power over bodies, before it describes freedom.

passages.title: Moses preserved and exiled
passages.summary: Moses's mother hides him. Pharaoh's daughter adopts him. He later kills an Egyptian and flees.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses 1 expands Moses's later encounter with God. Keep that account distinct from his childhood.

contextNote.title: Women cross the boundaries that Pharaoh tries to enforce
contextNote.text: The king orders death, but women from both peoples preserve Moses. Pharaoh's daughter recognizes the child as Hebrew before adopting him. Her decision interrupts the ruler's attempt to control the next generation. Moses' later violence shows that rescue does not make his own judgment consistently sound.

passages.title: The burning bush
passages.summary: God calls Moses at Horeb. Moses must confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Moses's call as preparation for prophetic service.

contextNote.title: God's attention begins with the workers' suffering
contextNote.text: The call begins with what God sees and hears in Egypt. Moses' task follows that attention to people under forced labor. His questions reveal the distance between a vast need and one person's confidence. The promised presence answers that distance without making Moses the source of deliverance.

passages.title: Moses returns
passages.summary: God gives Moses signs. Aaron joins him. Zipporah acts during a dangerous encounter.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how help from others can accompany an assignment from God.

contextNote.title: A difficult calling makes room for shared speech
contextNote.text: Moses repeatedly questions his ability to speak before others. Aaron's role gives the mission another voice rather than removing Moses. The signs also answer the problem of being believed. Authority here requires communication and cooperation, not simply receiving a private command.

passages.title: Pharaoh increases the burden
passages.summary: Moses and Aaron ask for release. Pharaoh withholds straw but demands the same brick count.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the strain of trusting a promise when conditions first become worse.

contextNote.title: The ruler makes the workers pay for the request
contextNote.text: Pharaoh calls the request for worship evidence of laziness. He then increases the burden without reducing the required output. The policy turns workers against the people asking for their release. Moses' complaint shows how a promised rescue can initially deepen a community's distress.

passages.title: God renews the promise
passages.summary: God promises deliverance and covenant belonging. A family record identifies Moses and Aaron.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The covenant promise includes belonging to God. Consider hope without blaming those exhausted by suffering.

contextNote.title: Harsh labor changes what the people can hear
contextNote.text: The promise reaches people whose work has left them unable to listen. Their response is not described simply as a lack of belief. The family record then locates the messengers within this suffering people. Deliverance must address damaged lives as well as supply persuasive words.

passages.title: Staff and river
passages.summary: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent. The Nile's water turns to blood.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the effects of a ruler's refusal on the people under his power.

contextNote.title: The conflict reaches the water that sustains daily life
contextNote.text: The Nile's changed water carries the dispute beyond Pharaoh's court. Drinking, fishing, and ordinary survival enter the struggle over release. Similar acts by the royal magicians do not supply clean water. The account distinguishes reproducing a sign from answering the suffering it causes.

passages.title: Frogs, lice, and flies
passages.summary: Three plagues strike Egypt. Pharaoh promises relief and then changes his decision.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your promises remain firm when immediate pressure ends.

contextNote.title: Permission offered under pressure remains restricted
contextNote.text: Pharaoh offers worship while trying to limit how far the people can go. His concessions preserve a claim over their movement. Relief then removes the pressure that produced his promise. The repeated pattern makes the ruler's words unreliable as a basis for freedom.

passages.title: Livestock, boils, and hail
passages.summary: Further plagues affect animals and people. Some Egyptians heed the warning about hail.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how repentance differs from a statement made only to end pain.

contextNote.title: People within Egypt do not respond in one way
contextNote.text: Some of Pharaoh's servants shelter workers and livestock after the warning. Others leave them exposed. The distinction places a real choice within the threatened population. The account separates the king's refusal from the varied responses of people under his authority.

passages.title: Locusts and darkness
passages.summary: Pharaoh rejects full release. Locusts consume crops. Darkness covers Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how worship can require more than a restricted permission from a ruler.

contextNote.title: Control continues through what the people must leave behind
contextNote.text: Pharaoh permits people to go but tries to keep their livestock. Moses explains that worship requires resources the ruler would retain. The dispute concerns the practical means to leave, not only permission in words. Each limited offer reveals another form of continued dependence.

passages.title: The final plague announced
passages.summary: Moses announces the death of the firstborn. Pharaoh still refuses release.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do the deaths in this chapter affect your understanding of Israel's freedom?

contextNote.title: Royal refusal creates danger beyond the royal household
contextNote.text: The warning names households across Egypt's unequal social positions. The ruler's decision therefore has consequences for people who do not share his power. The final plague cannot be read only as a contest between two leaders. Its stated reach introduces grief throughout the land before departure begins.

passages.title: Passover and departure
passages.summary: Israel keeps Passover. The firstborn die. Pharaoh releases the people. They leave Rameses.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the Passover lamb with Jesus Christ. Study the sign and the remembered deliverance.

contextNote.title: A meal makes departure available to later generations
contextNote.text: The instructions anticipate children asking about a ritual they did not witness beginning. A household answer links the meal with deliverance from Egypt. Memory will therefore depend on repeated food, speech, and practice. The same chapter preserves Egyptian grief beside Israel's account of freedom.

passages.title: Remembering and the pillars
passages.summary: God commands remembrance of the firstborn and unleavened bread. Cloud and fire lead the people.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how repeated worship can teach children about God's deliverance.

contextNote.title: The journey accounts for fear as well as distance
contextNote.text: The selected route avoids a war that could send the people back. A shorter journey would not necessarily sustain their new freedom. Teaching about bread and the firstborn also addresses the future beyond this travel. Departure requires both a usable path and practices that preserve its meaning.

passages.title: The sea crossing
passages.summary: Pharaoh pursues Israel. Moses stretches out his hand. Israel crosses and the army is overwhelmed.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: First Nephi 17 recalls the sea crossing to teach trust in God.

contextNote.title: Fear makes the old dependence appear safer
contextNote.text: The approaching army changes how the people describe their departure. Service in Egypt now seems preferable to death in the wilderness. Their complaint recalls the cost of freedom before a safe route appears. The crossing answers a danger that the people cannot remove through their own strength.

passages.title: Songs and bitter water
passages.summary: Moses and Miriam lead songs. The people reach bitter water and then Elim.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how gratitude and present needs can both appear in a life of faith.

contextNote.title: The song ends before the need for water ends
contextNote.text: Victory receives a public song led by voices from the rescued community. Bitter water then returns attention to the needs of bodies. Praise does not remove the practical demands of travel. The chapter places celebrated deliverance beside another test of whether life can continue outside Egypt.

passages.title: Manna and Sabbath
passages.summary: God provides manna and quail. The people gather food daily and rest on the Sabbath.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects manna with reliance on God. Consider daily preparation and Sabbath rest.

contextNote.title: Food becomes a test of community
contextNote.text: Gathering manna tests more than belief in a miracle. The rules limit stored food and require rest. Those with more cannot keep an endless surplus. Hunger exposes whether the people can trust daily provision. Freedom requires learning a different way to live together.

passages.title: Water and Amalek
passages.summary: God provides water at Rephidim. Joshua leads the fight against Amalek while others support Moses.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider why support for others belongs alongside individual faith.

contextNote.title: The battle depends on support that the account makes visible
contextNote.text: Joshua fights while Moses holds up his hands. When Moses tires, Aaron and Hur support him. This arrangement gives several forms of work a place within one outcome. The account does not reduce survival to a single leader acting alone.

passages.title: Jethro's counsel
passages.summary: Jethro visits Moses. He advises shared responsibility for judging the people's disputes.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how wise counsel can improve service and reduce an unfair burden.

contextNote.title: Accessible judgment requires more than one capable leader
contextNote.text: Jethro considers the strain on Moses and on those waiting for decisions. Shared responsibility shortens that dependence on a single person. Difficult cases remain with Moses, while others receive local attention. The advice concerns how an institution serves people, not merely how its leader saves time.

passages.title: At Sinai
passages.summary: Israel reaches Sinai. God offers a covenant. The people prepare for God's presence.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects covenant belonging with duties of holiness and service.

contextNote.title: A rescued people must answer an offered relationship
contextNote.text: The covenant proposal follows the reminder of rescue from Egypt. The people answer before the detailed commands arrive. Their response turns a shared deliverance into a shared obligation. Preparation and boundaries then mark the seriousness of the encounter they have agreed to enter.

passages.title: The Ten Commandments
passages.summary: God gives commands about worship and relationships. The people fear the encounter.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies how each command can shape faithful choices.

contextNote.title: Rest limits the household's power over others
contextNote.text: The command names servants, animals, and resident foreigners alongside the household itself. The person controlling their work must also allow their rest. This places a boundary around economic power inside an ordinary home. Worship therefore includes how people treat those whose time they can command.

passages.title: Laws about servants and injury
passages.summary: The laws address servitude, violence, and responsibility for injury.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the difference between an ancient legal setting and present moral duties toward people.

contextNote.title: Injury rules reveal both protection and unequal status
contextNote.text: The laws distinguish servants from free people in several cases. A servant's damaged eye or tooth can lead to release. That protection operates within a system that still permits human ownership. Read the specific restraint without treating the chapter as an end to unequal power.

passages.title: Property and vulnerable people
passages.summary: The laws address theft, damaged property, loans, and care for strangers, widows, and orphans.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: How can memories of need help you care for others?

contextNote.title: A loan cannot remove the borrower's means to endure the night
contextNote.text: The cloak rule limits how a lender uses security for repayment. The garment must return because the borrower needs it to sleep. Property rights therefore face a claim arising from bodily need. The surrounding warnings about vulnerable people make economic power a concern of divine judgment.

passages.title: Justice, rest, and festivals
passages.summary: God commands honest judgment, rest, and annual feasts. An angel will lead Israel.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your worship also changes your judgment and treatment of others.

contextNote.title: An enemy's need can interrupt personal hostility
contextNote.text: The instruction requires help for an enemy's overloaded animal. The dispute between owners does not cancel responsibility toward a suffering creature. Nearby rules also reject false testimony and unequal treatment in court. Justice includes actions that resist both friendship-based favors and revenge.

passages.title: The covenant confirmed
passages.summary: Moses reads the covenant terms. Israel accepts them. Moses ascends the mountain.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: A covenant includes an informed promise. Consider the duties that follow your agreement with God.

contextNote.title: The agreement follows a public reading of its terms
contextNote.text: Moses reads the covenant book before the people's response. Their commitment is attached to stated words rather than an undefined loyalty. Blood and a shared meal then give the agreement visible form. The scene joins hearing, consent, and practice within one shared relationship.

passages.title: The ark, table, and lampstand
passages.summary: God gives plans for a sanctuary and its furnishings.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the tabernacle with worship and God's presence among His people.

contextNote.title: The sanctuary brings presence into a traveling community
contextNote.text: The proposed dwelling follows rescue and the covenant agreement. Gifts come from people willing to contribute rather than from Pharaoh's forced labor. Furnishings provide ordered places for testimony, food, and light. The design places God's presence among the people without making their leader its owner.

passages.title: The tabernacle structure
passages.summary: God specifies curtains, frames, coverings, and the inner veil.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how a prepared space can support reverence without replacing faithful conduct.

contextNote.title: A veil gives the tent an ordered interior
contextNote.text: The instructions distinguish the holy place from the most holy place. Curtains and frames therefore organize access as well as support a structure. The repeated measurements connect sacred boundaries with skilled material work. A portable dwelling still requires clear differences between its spaces.

passages.title: Altar, court, and light
passages.summary: God gives plans for the altar, courtyard, and daily lamp oil.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the repeated work that sustains a place of worship.

contextNote.title: Continuing light requires continuing contributions
contextNote.text: The people supply oil while priests tend the lamp. The sanctuary's light depends on recurring work after construction ends. The courtyard also defines how the larger community approaches the dwelling. Building the place is therefore the start of shared responsibility, not its completion.

passages.title: The priests' clothing
passages.summary: God directs the making of Aaron's garments and the breastpiece bearing Israel's names.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider what it means to carry other people's needs within sacred service.

contextNote.title: The priest carries names rather than only personal status
contextNote.text: Aaron's breastpiece places the tribes' names over his heart. His clothing connects his approach to God with the people he represents. The garments make that representative duty visible through crafted materials. Distinct clothing grants a role whose purpose reaches beyond the person wearing it.

passages.title: Consecrating the priests
passages.summary: God gives instructions to appoint priests and make daily offerings.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies preparation for sacred service. Consider the duties beyond a title.

contextNote.title: Priestly preparation serves a larger purpose of presence
contextNote.text: Washing, clothing, and offerings set the priests apart for their work. These actions do not make the sanctuary an end in itself. The closing explanation returns to God's dwelling among the rescued people. Detailed ritual therefore belongs within the larger account of departure and shared life.

passages.title: Incense, washing, and sacred oil
passages.summary: God gives instructions for incense, washing, the census payment, and sacred oil.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how preparation can support worship without becoming only an outward routine.

contextNote.title: A required payment does not measure people by their wealth
contextNote.text: The census payment assigns the same amount to rich and poor people. Within this rule, greater wealth does not purchase a greater share in belonging. Other instructions reserve oils and incense for stated uses. The chapter distinguishes common obligation from materials whose use remains restricted.

passages.title: Skilled workers and Sabbath
passages.summary: God appoints Bezalel and Oholiab. The Sabbath remains a covenant sign. Moses receives tablets.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how creative skill and Sabbath observance can both serve God.

contextNote.title: Sacred construction does not cancel the command to rest
contextNote.text: The account names workers whose skills can carry out the design. It then repeats the Sabbath requirement before the work begins. Even the task of building a sanctuary has a limit on labor. Skill, devotion, and urgency do not authorize endless work.

passages.title: The golden calf
passages.summary: Aaron makes the calf. Moses intercedes, breaks the tablets, and confronts the camp.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how quick substitutes for trust can damage a covenant relationship.

contextNote.title: Freedom does not remove the desire for visible gods
contextNote.text: The people want a god they can see and follow. Aaron uses a familiar animal form to answer that demand. The conflict concerns worship, leadership, and the terms of the covenant. The calf does not solve their fear of Moses’ absence. A visible object can still leave the community without direction.

passages.title: Moses seeks God's presence
passages.summary: Moses meets with God outside the camp. He asks for guidance and God's continuing presence.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your requests seek God's companionship as well as a desired outcome.

contextNote.title: Arrival alone would not complete the purpose of rescue
contextNote.text: Moses asks that God's presence accompany the journey. The destination would not distinguish this people without that relationship. The tent outside the camp makes separation visible after the calf crisis. The conversation therefore concerns restored belonging as well as continued movement.

passages.title: The covenant renewed
passages.summary: God declares mercy and justice. New tablets are given. Moses returns with a shining face.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual reads renewal alongside repentance. Consider mercy with continuing responsibility.

contextNote.title: Renewal holds mercy beside continuing consequences
contextNote.text: God's declaration names compassion and forgiveness while also naming responsibility for wrongdoing. The new tablets follow the broken ones rather than erasing that history. The people receive terms for life after their failure. Restoration here requires renewed practice, not only relief from punishment.

passages.title: Gifts and willing work
passages.summary: Moses teaches Sabbath rest. The people bring materials. Skilled workers begin their tasks.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how willingness and varied skills can build a worshiping community.

contextNote.title: Willing labor contrasts with the labor that began the book
contextNote.text: The people bring gifts and offer skills for a dwelling among them. Women and men appear within the account of contributions. This work follows an explicit reminder to rest. Read it beside Pharaoh's demands, which joined forced output with disregard for the workers' lives.

passages.title: More than enough
passages.summary: The gifts exceed the need. The workers build the tabernacle's curtains, frames, and veil.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how wise stewardship includes knowing when a collection has met its need.

contextNote.title: A finished purpose sets a limit on collecting gifts
contextNote.text: The workers report that supplies exceed what the task requires. Moses then stops further contributions. Generosity does not justify collecting without an end. The command links what people give with the work those gifts actually support.

passages.title: The furnishings made
passages.summary: Bezalel makes the ark, table, lampstand, and incense altar.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the place of careful work in fulfilling a sacred responsibility.

contextNote.title: Repeated details connect a plan with its fulfillment
contextNote.text: The account now describes making objects that earlier chapters specified. This repetition lets the reader compare instructions with actions. Named skilled work turns commands into a physical place for worship. Completion depends on careful labor rather than the mere announcement of a design.

passages.title: Altar, court, and accounts
passages.summary: The workers build the outer furnishings. The chapter records the materials used.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how clear records and accountable service can support trust.

contextNote.title: Sacred work includes an account of its materials
contextNote.text: The record names responsibility for counting materials used in the dwelling. Such accounting sits beside descriptions of completed objects. Gifts for worship still require explanation of where resources went. The named workers also prevent the finished structure from hiding the labor that produced it.

passages.title: Garments and inspection
passages.summary: The workers finish the priests' clothing. Moses inspects the completed work and blesses them.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how careful review can honor the work of those who serve.

contextNote.title: A blessing follows examination of completed work
contextNote.text: Moses looks at the finished work before blessing its makers. The repeated statement about following instructions gives the examination its standard. Clothing and furnishings together prepare the dwelling for use. The account values completion that can be inspected, not only good intentions at the start.

passages.title: The tabernacle raised
passages.summary: Moses sets up the sanctuary. God's glory fills it. Cloud and fire guide later journeys.
passages.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the sanctuary with God's presence. Consider worship as part of the journey after deliverance.

contextNote.title: The completed dwelling still belongs to a moving people
contextNote.text: The cloud determines when the people travel and when they remain. Their built sanctuary does not end the journey or establish permanent settlement. Presence now accompanies their movement through the wilderness. The ending answers the book's opening bondage with guidance that reaches beyond departure.

events.title: Oppression and the midwives
events.summary: A new king enslaves Israel. Shiphrah and Puah refuse his order to kill boys.
events.detail: Pharaoh treats a growing people as a threat. He turns that fear into forced work and killing. The store cities serve royal interests. The women resist through small acts that preserve life. The book begins with power over bodies, before it describes freedom.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how reverence for God can require resistance to cruelty.

events.title: Moses preserved and exiled
events.summary: Moses's mother hides him. Pharaoh's daughter adopts him. He later kills an Egyptian and flees.
events.detail: The king orders death, but women from both peoples preserve Moses. Pharaoh's daughter recognizes the child as Hebrew before adopting him. Her decision interrupts the ruler's attempt to control the next generation. Moses' later violence shows that rescue does not make his own judgment consistently sound.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Moses 1 expands Moses's later encounter with God. Keep that account distinct from his childhood.

events.title: The burning bush
events.summary: God calls Moses at Horeb. Moses must confront Pharaoh and lead Israel out.
events.detail: The call begins with what God sees and hears in Egypt. Moses' task follows that attention to people under forced labor. His questions reveal the distance between a vast need and one person's confidence. The promised presence answers that distance without making Moses the source of deliverance.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual reads Moses's call as preparation for prophetic service.

events.title: Moses returns
events.summary: God gives Moses signs. Aaron joins him. Zipporah acts during a dangerous encounter.
events.detail: Moses repeatedly questions his ability to speak before others. Aaron's role gives the mission another voice rather than removing Moses. The signs also answer the problem of being believed. Authority here requires communication and cooperation, not simply receiving a private command.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how help from others can accompany an assignment from God.

events.title: Pharaoh increases the burden
events.summary: Moses and Aaron ask for release. Pharaoh withholds straw but demands the same brick count.
events.detail: Pharaoh calls the request for worship evidence of laziness. He then increases the burden without reducing the required output. The policy turns workers against the people asking for their release. Moses' complaint shows how a promised rescue can initially deepen a community's distress.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the strain of trusting a promise when conditions first become worse.

events.title: God renews the promise
events.summary: God promises deliverance and covenant belonging. A family record identifies Moses and Aaron.
events.detail: The promise reaches people whose work has left them unable to listen. Their response is not described simply as a lack of belief. The family record then locates the messengers within this suffering people. Deliverance must address damaged lives as well as supply persuasive words.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The covenant promise includes belonging to God. Consider hope without blaming those exhausted by suffering.

events.title: Staff and river
events.summary: Aaron's staff becomes a serpent. The Nile's water turns to blood.
events.detail: The Nile's changed water carries the dispute beyond Pharaoh's court. Drinking, fishing, and ordinary survival enter the struggle over release. Similar acts by the royal magicians do not supply clean water. The account distinguishes reproducing a sign from answering the suffering it causes.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the effects of a ruler's refusal on the people under his power.

events.title: Frogs, lice, and flies
events.summary: Three plagues strike Egypt. Pharaoh promises relief and then changes his decision.
events.detail: Pharaoh offers worship while trying to limit how far the people can go. His concessions preserve a claim over their movement. Relief then removes the pressure that produced his promise. The repeated pattern makes the ruler's words unreliable as a basis for freedom.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your promises remain firm when immediate pressure ends.

events.title: Livestock, boils, and hail
events.summary: Further plagues affect animals and people. Some Egyptians heed the warning about hail.
events.detail: Some of Pharaoh's servants shelter workers and livestock after the warning. Others leave them exposed. The distinction places a real choice within the threatened population. The account separates the king's refusal from the varied responses of people under his authority.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how repentance differs from a statement made only to end pain.

events.title: Locusts and darkness
events.summary: Pharaoh rejects full release. Locusts consume crops. Darkness covers Egypt.
events.detail: Pharaoh permits people to go but tries to keep their livestock. Moses explains that worship requires resources the ruler would retain. The dispute concerns the practical means to leave, not only permission in words. Each limited offer reveals another form of continued dependence.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how worship can require more than a restricted permission from a ruler.

events.title: The final plague announced
events.summary: Moses announces the death of the firstborn. Pharaoh still refuses release.
events.detail: The warning names households across Egypt's unequal social positions. The ruler's decision therefore has consequences for people who do not share his power. The final plague cannot be read only as a contest between two leaders. Its stated reach introduces grief throughout the land before departure begins.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: How do the deaths in this chapter affect your understanding of Israel's freedom?

events.title: Passover and departure
events.summary: Israel keeps Passover. The firstborn die. Pharaoh releases the people. They leave Rameses.
events.detail: The instructions anticipate children asking about a ritual they did not witness beginning. A household answer links the meal with deliverance from Egypt. Memory will therefore depend on repeated food, speech, and practice. The same chapter preserves Egyptian grief beside Israel's account of freedom.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the Passover lamb with Jesus Christ. Study the sign and the remembered deliverance.

events.title: Remembering and the pillars
events.summary: God commands remembrance of the firstborn and unleavened bread. Cloud and fire lead the people.
events.detail: The selected route avoids a war that could send the people back. A shorter journey would not necessarily sustain their new freedom. Teaching about bread and the firstborn also addresses the future beyond this travel. Departure requires both a usable path and practices that preserve its meaning.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how repeated worship can teach children about God's deliverance.

events.title: The sea crossing
events.summary: Pharaoh pursues Israel. Moses stretches out his hand. Israel crosses and the army is overwhelmed.
events.detail: The approaching army changes how the people describe their departure. Service in Egypt now seems preferable to death in the wilderness. Their complaint recalls the cost of freedom before a safe route appears. The crossing answers a danger that the people cannot remove through their own strength.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: First Nephi 17 recalls the sea crossing to teach trust in God.

events.title: Songs and bitter water
events.summary: Moses and Miriam lead songs. The people reach bitter water and then Elim.
events.detail: Victory receives a public song led by voices from the rescued community. Bitter water then returns attention to the needs of bodies. Praise does not remove the practical demands of travel. The chapter places celebrated deliverance beside another test of whether life can continue outside Egypt.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how gratitude and present needs can both appear in a life of faith.

events.title: Manna and Sabbath
events.summary: God provides manna and quail. The people gather food daily and rest on the Sabbath.
events.detail: Gathering manna tests more than belief in a miracle. The rules limit stored food and require rest. Those with more cannot keep an endless surplus. Hunger exposes whether the people can trust daily provision. Freedom requires learning a different way to live together.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects manna with reliance on God. Consider daily preparation and Sabbath rest.

events.title: Water and Amalek
events.summary: God provides water at Rephidim. Joshua leads the fight against Amalek while others support Moses.
events.detail: Joshua fights while Moses holds up his hands. When Moses tires, Aaron and Hur support him. This arrangement gives several forms of work a place within one outcome. The account does not reduce survival to a single leader acting alone.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider why support for others belongs alongside individual faith.

events.title: Jethro's counsel
events.summary: Jethro visits Moses. He advises shared responsibility for judging the people's disputes.
events.detail: Jethro considers the strain on Moses and on those waiting for decisions. Shared responsibility shortens that dependence on a single person. Difficult cases remain with Moses, while others receive local attention. The advice concerns how an institution serves people, not merely how its leader saves time.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how wise counsel can improve service and reduce an unfair burden.

events.title: At Sinai
events.summary: Israel reaches Sinai. God offers a covenant. The people prepare for God's presence.
events.detail: The covenant proposal follows the reminder of rescue from Egypt. The people answer before the detailed commands arrive. Their response turns a shared deliverance into a shared obligation. Preparation and boundaries then mark the seriousness of the encounter they have agreed to enter.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects covenant belonging with duties of holiness and service.

events.title: The Ten Commandments
events.summary: God gives commands about worship and relationships. The people fear the encounter.
events.detail: The command names servants, animals, and resident foreigners alongside the household itself. The person controlling their work must also allow their rest. This places a boundary around economic power inside an ordinary home. Worship therefore includes how people treat those whose time they can command.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies how each command can shape faithful choices.

events.title: Laws about servants and injury
events.summary: The laws address servitude, violence, and responsibility for injury.
events.detail: The laws distinguish servants from free people in several cases. A servant's damaged eye or tooth can lead to release. That protection operates within a system that still permits human ownership. Read the specific restraint without treating the chapter as an end to unequal power.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the difference between an ancient legal setting and present moral duties toward people.

events.title: Property and vulnerable people
events.summary: The laws address theft, damaged property, loans, and care for strangers, widows, and orphans.
events.detail: The cloak rule limits how a lender uses security for repayment. The garment must return because the borrower needs it to sleep. Property rights therefore face a claim arising from bodily need. The surrounding warnings about vulnerable people make economic power a concern of divine judgment.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: How can memories of need help you care for others?

events.title: Justice, rest, and festivals
events.summary: God commands honest judgment, rest, and annual feasts. An angel will lead Israel.
events.detail: The instruction requires help for an enemy's overloaded animal. The dispute between owners does not cancel responsibility toward a suffering creature. Nearby rules also reject false testimony and unequal treatment in court. Justice includes actions that resist both friendship-based favors and revenge.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your worship also changes your judgment and treatment of others.

events.title: The covenant confirmed
events.summary: Moses reads the covenant terms. Israel accepts them. Moses ascends the mountain.
events.detail: Moses reads the covenant book before the people's response. Their commitment is attached to stated words rather than an undefined loyalty. Blood and a shared meal then give the agreement visible form. The scene joins hearing, consent, and practice within one shared relationship.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: A covenant includes an informed promise. Consider the duties that follow your agreement with God.

events.title: The ark, table, and lampstand
events.summary: God gives plans for a sanctuary and its furnishings.
events.detail: The proposed dwelling follows rescue and the covenant agreement. Gifts come from people willing to contribute rather than from Pharaoh's forced labor. Furnishings provide ordered places for testimony, food, and light. The design places God's presence among the people without making their leader its owner.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual connects the tabernacle with worship and God's presence among His people.

events.title: The tabernacle structure
events.summary: God specifies curtains, frames, coverings, and the inner veil.
events.detail: The instructions distinguish the holy place from the most holy place. Curtains and frames therefore organize access as well as support a structure. The repeated measurements connect sacred boundaries with skilled material work. A portable dwelling still requires clear differences between its spaces.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how a prepared space can support reverence without replacing faithful conduct.

events.title: Altar, court, and light
events.summary: God gives plans for the altar, courtyard, and daily lamp oil.
events.detail: The people supply oil while priests tend the lamp. The sanctuary's light depends on recurring work after construction ends. The courtyard also defines how the larger community approaches the dwelling. Building the place is therefore the start of shared responsibility, not its completion.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider the repeated work that sustains a place of worship.

events.title: The priests' clothing
events.summary: God directs the making of Aaron's garments and the breastpiece bearing Israel's names.
events.detail: Aaron's breastpiece places the tribes' names over his heart. His clothing connects his approach to God with the people he represents. The garments make that representative duty visible through crafted materials. Distinct clothing grants a role whose purpose reaches beyond the person wearing it.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider what it means to carry other people's needs within sacred service.

events.title: Consecrating the priests
events.summary: God gives instructions to appoint priests and make daily offerings.
events.detail: Washing, clothing, and offerings set the priests apart for their work. These actions do not make the sanctuary an end in itself. The closing explanation returns to God's dwelling among the rescued people. Detailed ritual therefore belongs within the larger account of departure and shared life.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: The Church manual studies preparation for sacred service. Consider the duties beyond a title.

events.title: Incense, washing, and sacred oil
events.summary: God gives instructions for incense, washing, the census payment, and sacred oil.
events.detail: The census payment assigns the same amount to rich and poor people. Within this rule, greater wealth does not purchase a greater share in belonging. Other instructions reserve oils and incense for stated uses. The chapter distinguishes common obligation from materials whose use remains restricted.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how preparation can support worship without becoming only an outward routine.

events.title: Skilled workers and Sabbath
events.summary: God appoints Bezalel and Oholiab. The Sabbath remains a covenant sign. Moses receives tablets.
events.detail: The account names workers whose skills can carry out the design. It then repeats the Sabbath requirement before the work begins. Even the task of building a sanctuary has a limit on labor. Skill, devotion, and urgency do not authorize endless work.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how creative skill and Sabbath observance can both serve God.

events.title: The golden calf
events.summary: Aaron makes the calf. Moses intercedes, breaks the tablets, and confronts the camp.
events.detail: The people want a god they can see and follow. Aaron uses a familiar animal form to answer that demand. The conflict concerns worship, leadership, and the terms of the covenant. The calf does not solve their fear of Moses’ absence. A visible object can still leave the community without direction.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider how quick substitutes for trust can damage a covenant relationship.

events.title: Moses seeks God's presence
events.summary: Moses meets with God outside the camp. He asks for guidance and God's continuing presence.
events.detail: Moses asks that God's presence accompany the journey. The destination would not distinguish this people without that relationship. The tent outside the camp makes separation visible after the calf crisis. The conversation therefore concerns restored belonging as well as continued movement.
events.uncertainty: Site markers follow a traditional regional reading. Many campsites and the sea crossing remain uncertain.

lds.text: Consider whether your requests seek God's companionship as well as a desired outcome.

events.title: The covenant renewed
events.summary: God declares mercy and justice. New tablets are given. Moses returns with a shining face.
events.detail: God's declaration names compassion and forgiveness while also naming responsibility for wrongdoing. The new tablets follow the broken ones rather than erasing that history. The people receive terms for life after their failure. Restoration here requires renewed practice, not only relief from punishment.

guides.title: Exodus: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Forced work and fear
steps.text: Pharaoh treats a growing people as a threat. He turns that fear into forced work and killing. The store cities serve royal interests. The women resist through small acts that preserve life. The book begins with power over bodies, before it describes freedom.

steps.title: Food becomes a test of community
steps.text: Gathering manna tests more than belief in a miracle. The rules limit stored food and require rest. Those with more cannot keep an endless surplus. Hunger exposes whether the people can trust daily provision. Freedom requires learning a different way to live together.

steps.title: Freedom does not remove the desire for visible gods
steps.text: The people want a god they can see and follow. Aaron uses a familiar animal form to answer that demand. The conflict concerns worship, leadership, and the terms of the covenant. The calf does not solve their fear of Moses’ absence. A visible object can still leave the community without direction.

textRoutes.title: Moses preserved and exiled
textRoutes.summary: Moses's mother hides him. Pharaoh's daughter adopts him. He later kills an Egyptian and flees.
textRoutes.detail: The king orders death, but women from both peoples preserve Moses. Pharaoh's daughter recognizes the child as Hebrew before adopting him. Her decision interrupts the ruler's attempt to control the next generation. Moses' later violence shows that rescue does not make his own judgment consistently sound.

textRoutes.title: Moses returns
textRoutes.summary: God gives Moses signs. Aaron joins him. Zipporah acts during a dangerous encounter.
textRoutes.detail: Moses repeatedly questions his ability to speak before others. Aaron's role gives the mission another voice rather than removing Moses. The signs also answer the problem of being believed. Authority here requires communication and cooperation, not simply receiving a private command.

textRoutes.title: Passover and departure
textRoutes.summary: Israel keeps Passover. The firstborn die. Pharaoh releases the people. They leave Rameses.
textRoutes.detail: The instructions anticipate children asking about a ritual they did not witness beginning. A household answer links the meal with deliverance from Egypt. Memory will therefore depend on repeated food, speech, and practice. The same chapter preserves Egyptian grief beside Israel's account of freedom.

textRoutes.title: Remembering and the pillars
textRoutes.summary: God commands remembrance of the firstborn and unleavened bread. Cloud and fire lead the people.
textRoutes.detail: The selected route avoids a war that could send the people back. A shorter journey would not necessarily sustain their new freedom. Teaching about bread and the firstborn also addresses the future beyond this travel. Departure requires both a usable path and practices that preserve its meaning.
